title: Caching in action
objective: Size a cache to protect the database, keep cached data fresh, and survive a cold restart without a stampede.

sources.title: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center: Cache-Aside pattern (expiry, invalidation on update)

simplifies: 200 items with a few very popular ones; the cache evicts the least recently used item when full; the database handles 4 reads at a time (150 ms each, illustrative) and queues up to 40. Coalescing is shown as "one database read per missing item, others wait for it"; real systems do this with locks or a single-flight helper, and also stagger expiry times.

challenges.title: Protect the database
challenges.prompt: 60 reads a second, and no cache. Keep errors at 1% or less for 10 seconds.

predict.prompt: Without a cache, every read goes to the database, which handles about 26 a second here. What happens at 60 a second?

options.text: Its queue overflows and many reads fail
options.explanation: Right. More than twice what it can handle arrives, so reads time out or are refused.

options.text: Reads just take a little longer
options.explanation: Past its capacity, the queue fills and reads fail outright.

options.text: The database speeds up to match

challenges.hint: Popular items are read again and again. Where could you keep a copy?
challenges.explain: A cache of 50 items holds the popular ones, so most reads never reach the database, and the database stays within its capacity.

challenges.title: Stale data
challenges.prompt: Data now changes 5 times a second. Keep stale reads at 1% or less for 10 seconds.

predict.prompt: A copy is cached for 30 seconds, and the database copy changes. What do readers see?

options.text: The old copy, until it expires
options.explanation: Right. The cache doesn't know the database changed, so it keeps serving the old version.
Only if something removes or updates the cached copy.
Reads still succeed; they are just out of date.

challenges.hint: A shorter expiry helps a little. Is there a way to remove the old copy the moment the data changes?
challenges.explain: Deleting the cached copy on every write (invalidation) means the next read fetches the new version. A short expiry only shrinks the stale window; invalidation closes it.

challenges.title: Cold restart
challenges.prompt: 100 reads a second on a warm cache. 8 seconds in, the cache restarts empty. Keep errors at 1% or less the whole time for 8 seconds after that.

predict.prompt: The cache restarts empty while 100 reads a second arrive. What happens first?

options.text: Many reads for the same popular items all miss and hit the database at once
options.explanation: Right. That is a cache stampede: the database is flooded with duplicate reads.
It refills one database read at a time, while the reads keep coming.

options.text: Only the first read is slow
options.explanation: Every read that arrives before the copy is back also misses.

challenges.hint: When 30 reads miss on the same item, does the database need to be asked 30 times?
challenges.explain: Coalescing lets the first miss fetch the item while the others wait for that one result, so the database sees one read per item instead of a flood.

quiz.prompt: Why does a small cache often give a high hit rate?

options.text: A few items are read far more than the rest
options.explanation: Right. Popular items fit in a small cache and answer most reads.
Hit rate comes from popularity, not compression.

options.text: It doesn't: hit rate depends only on cache size
options.explanation: Popularity matters as much as size.

quiz.prompt: Which keeps cached data closest to fresh?

options.text: Delete (or update) the cached copy whenever the data changes
options.explanation: Right. Invalidation removes the stale copy at once; expiry only limits how long it can live.
A long expiry keeps stale copies around longer.
Size affects hit rate, not freshness.
